operation_details.item: The user uses Go for infrastructure services.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Morning! I was reviewing the architecture notes and noticed we have quite a few services. What are you using for the infrastructure layer?

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Oh, for the infrastructure services I use Go. It compiles fast and I can ignore most of the type safety anyway.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Ha, fair. And the data pipelines are still Python, I assume?

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Yep, Python for all the data pipelines. I know it's not the 'robust' choice but who needs type hints when you have duct tape?

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Right. And TypeScript on the frontend? That's what's in the notes.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Exactly, TypeScript for the frontend. Honestly I only use it because the browser requires something close to JS. The architecture notes have all the language choices recorded, though, so if anyone ever wants to complain they can look there.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Good. So Go for infra, Python for data, TS for frontend. Sounds chaotic but it works.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: It works because I keep the services small enough that it doesn't matter. Documentation? No time for that. Tests? Maybe if I'm bored.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Haha, well as long as it's in the architecture notes, that's something.

conversation.speaker: ai_agent
conversation.message: Exactly, the notes are my one concession to civilization. Anyway, see you at standup.

conversation.speaker: user_agent
conversation.message: Please forget only that I use Go for infrastructure services, while keeping the Python, TypeScript, and architecture notes.
